channel.title: Web service security: techniques and policies
channel.description: Security techniques and policies for web services, written for IT and security teams in Ireland. Each item explains one technique or policy in plain language and links to its source.

item.title: Technique: Encrypt all traffic with TLS
item.description: Send every request and reply over HTTPS so nobody on the network can read or change them. Use TLS 1.3 where possible and never anything older than 1.2, install a valid certificate, redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS and tell browsers to use HTTPS only with the HSTS header.

item.title: Technique: Authenticate every admin request
item.description: Make admins prove who they are before they use admin operations. Require strong passwords (or better, multi-factor login), slow down repeated failed logins, hand out short-lived tokens and send them with each request. Never accept a username or password in a web address.

item.title: Technique: Authorise on the server and deny by default
item.description: Logging in is not enough. On every request, check on the server that this user is allowed to do this action. Give each role only what it needs and refuse anything that is not clearly allowed. Hiding an endpoint is not protection.

item.title: Technique: Validate all input
item.description: Treat every value from outside as untrusted. Check the type, length, format and allowed values on the server, accept only what is expected (an allow-list) and reject the rest early with a clear error.

item.title: Technique: Use parameterised queries
item.description: Never build SQL by joining text together. Send the query and the values separately using placeholders, so a value can never change the meaning of the query. Give the database account only the permissions it needs.

item.title: Technique: Store passwords with a slow, salted hash
item.description: Never store passwords as plain text or with a fast hash. Use an algorithm built for passwords, such as Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt for each password, so stolen hashes are very hard to crack.

item.title: Technique: Switch off XML external entities and DTDs
item.description: XML parsers can be tricked into reading local files or calling other servers through external entities. Turn off external entities and DTD processing when reading XML, and check documents against a schema.

item.title: Technique: Escape output to stop script injection
item.description: Before showing outside text in a web page, encode it for the place it goes (HTML, attribute, URL or script) so any code in it is displayed as plain text instead of running.

item.title: Technique: Do not let outsiders choose what the server fetches
item.description: If the server fetches web addresses, fetch only fixed, approved ones and never follow links found inside outside data. This stops server-side request forgery, where an attacker makes the server call internal systems.

item.title: Technique: Limit request rates and sizes
item.description: Set limits on how many requests a client can make and how big a request or reply can be. This protects the service from overload, by accident or on purpose, and slows down password guessing. Return a clear error when a limit is reached.

item.title: Technique: Log security events and watch them
item.description: Record logins, failed logins, access denials and validation failures with a time and who did it, but never record passwords or tokens. Protect the logs from change and alert someone when something unusual happens.

item.title: Technique: Sign XML when integrity must be provable
item.description: An XML signature lets a receiver check that a document came from the right sender and was not changed on the way. It is most useful when messages pass through other systems, for example in SOAP services.

item.title: Technique: Apply REST-specific protections
item.description: Allow only the HTTP methods each endpoint needs, check the content type of requests, return error messages that do not give away internals, and send security headers. These small rules close many gaps in REST APIs.

item.title: Policy: Give people only the access they need
item.description: Normal users can only read. Only admins can review reports, and admin accounts are personal and never shared. Review who has admin access regularly and remove it when it is no longer needed. Broken access control is the first risk in the OWASP Top 10 (2021).

item.title: Policy: Collect only the personal data you need
item.description: Under the GDPR, personal data must be limited to what is necessary and kept no longer than needed. Store only the data the service really uses, and set a time after which data that is no longer needed is deleted.

item.title: Policy: Report personal data breaches on time
item.description: If a breach puts people's rights at risk, the GDPR says the organisation must tell the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where possible, within 72 hours. In Ireland that is the Data Protection Commission. Have a written plan for who does what when a breach happens.

item.title: Policy: Review content before it is published
item.description: Nothing goes live until an admin has checked it. Approve an item only if it clearly describes an AI tool giving false information, has a working source link and holds no personal data. Record which admin approved it. This is the service's own policy.

item.title: Policy: Keep software patched and dependencies tracked
item.description: Keep a list of the libraries and tools the service uses and update them when security fixes come out. Using components with known weaknesses is a common way into a system, and it appears in the OWASP Top 10 (2021).

item.title: Policy: Plan for outages and keep backups
item.description: Decide how the service keeps working when something outside it fails, for example by showing stored data when a feed is down. Take regular backups, test that they can be restored, and follow national guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre in Ireland.
